headline: Paraguay's ousted president now faces criminal charges.
summary: Paraguay's Senate voted 44-0 on Friday to remove Santiago Peña, three days after regulators seized Ueno Bank and froze nearly 3 million customers out of their savings. Prosecutors ordered his arrest minutes later and questioned him Saturday on breach of trust. Lawmakers say he steered public money into the bank. He denies wrongdoing.
cover_answer: Stuck in a bank that got shut. Some is coming back.
table_question: If the referee owns part of a team, do you pull them off the field?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In Paraguay, a country in South America, a bank was shut down and 3 million people couldn't get to their money. The lawmakers voted that the president let it happen, so he lost his job. Picture a piggy bank with a lid that won't open; grown-ups are working to get it open. Nothing changes for you, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: The piggy bank that won't open is the one picture, and the arrest stays off the card. At six, one picture stands in for the event.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event and reads a parent's face before the words, so the script gives them a piggy bank with a stuck lid and leaves the arrest and the protests out. Expect "did they get it back?" Some have. More than a million people have part of it, and the new president promised the rest.

8-12.script: A bank in Paraguay collapsed, freezing nearly 3 million people's savings. Lawmakers say the president steered public money into it. Three days later the Senate voted 44-0 to remove him, and prosecutors ordered his arrest. Like a referee with a stake in one team: pulled off first, questions later.
8-12.why: Collapse, vote, arrest is a chain an 11-year-old can follow. The referee with a stake is the fairness call.
8-12.why_long: A 11-year-old is working out cause and effect and whether rules reach the people in charge, so the script runs the chain: the bank fails, regulators seize it, the Senate votes 44-0, prosecutors order the arrest. The referee with a stake in one team is the mechanism. Expect "did he steal it?" Lawmakers say so. He denies it.

13-17.script: If a president offers to resign, why refuse and remove him instead? Paraguay's Senate did, 44-0, so Santiago Peña loses the immunity ex-presidents keep; prosecutors ordered his arrest within minutes. Second: 1.2 million people have money back. 3 million lost access. Who covers the rest?
13-17.why: He offered to go. They refused so he could be tried. At 13 they hold both.
13-17.why_long: A 13-year-old can hold two true things, so the script gives both: Peña offered to resign, and the Senate refused so he would lose the immunity a resignation kept. The second question hands them the gap between 1.2 million reimbursed and 3 million frozen out, which no article settles. Expect "is he guilty?" Undecided. He denies it.

5-7.a: It's still in the bank, but the bank got shut and the doors are locked. Some people have part of it back already.

8-12.q: Why did the president get blamed?
8-12.a: He owned shares in its owner. Lawmakers say he steered public money in.

8-12.q: Can they really arrest a president?
8-12.a: Once the Senate removed him, yes. Prosecutors ordered it minutes later.

13-17.q: Why not just let him resign?
13-17.a: A resignation keeps his immunity. Removal strips it, so he can be tried.
His vice president, Pedro Alliana. He promised compensation.
